lesson_title: Shake the Cooldrink: Why Some Volcanoes Ooze and Others Explode
hook_text: Open it gently, it hisses. Shake it first, it goes everywhere. That's a volcano.
clip_script: Take a two-litre bottle of fizzy cooldrink. The gas is dissolved in there, invisible, under pressure. Open it gently and it hisses. Shake it first and it goes everywhere. Every volcano is that bottle. Molten rock underground has gas dissolved in it, and the gas wants out — the only question is how easily it can escape. Some magma is thin and runny, like warm honey off a spoon. Bubbles slide straight through and out, so nothing builds up. That volcano doesn't explode; it oozes. Red rivers of lava travel for kilometres and cool into wide, gently sloping ground — a shield volcano, like Hawaii. Other magma is thick, like cold stiff pap that fights the spoon. Bubbles can't get through, and the stuff is so stiff it corks its own pipe. Pressure builds behind that cork for years. When it finally gives, the top of the mountain is blown apart — and what comes out isn't a river, it's a blast of ash and rock. And you have seen the leftovers of this at home: every flat-topped koppie on the N1 is a hill wearing a hard dolerite hat, and the Drakensberg is nothing but lava, stacked sheet on sheet.
visual_style: A cooldrink bottle opening in slow motion, cutting to honey pouring off a spoon, then to stiff pap resisting, then to a wide aerial of Karoo koppies and the Drakensberg wall.
mood: Kitchen-table curiosity opening into landscape scale.
pacing: Playful and quick at the bottle, deliberate through the two magmas, expansive at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for volcano types, landforms and the hazards worth respecting.
